questions.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) - Cross-Cutting Concerns
questions.question: What is AOP in Spring?

answer.summary: AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) in Spring separates cross-cutting concerns like logging, security, and transaction management from core business logic by modularizing them into reusable aspects.

sections.title: What Is AOP and Why It Matters
sections.content:
Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) is a programming paradigm that complements Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) by providing a way to modularize **cross-cutting concerns** — functionality that spans across multiple classes and layers of an application.

In a typical enterprise application, certain behaviors like logging, security checks, transaction management, and performance monitoring cut across many components. Without AOP, you end up duplicating this code in every service method, violating the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle and making maintenance a nightmare.

Spring AOP solves this by letting you define these behaviors in a single place — called an **Aspect** — and then declaratively apply them to target methods without modifying the original code. Spring AOP uses **proxy-based** mechanism by default: it wraps your beans in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB proxy) and intercepts method calls to weave in the cross-cutting behavior at runtime.

sections.title: How Spring AOP Works Under the Hood
sections.content:
When Spring creates a bean that has AOP advice applied to it, it doesn't return the original object. Instead, it returns a **proxy object** that wraps the original. When code calls a method on this proxy, the proxy intercepts the call, runs the appropriate advice (before, after, or around the method), and then delegates to the actual target method.

Spring AOP supports two proxy strategies:

1. **JDK Dynamic Proxy** — used when the target implements an interface. The proxy implements the same interface and delegates calls.
2. **CGLIB Proxy** — used when the target class doesn't implement an interface. Spring creates a subclass of the target at runtime using bytecode generation.

This proxy-based approach has one important limitation: **self-invocation** (a method within the same class calling another method) bypasses the proxy, so AOP advice won't trigger. This is one of the most common gotchas in Spring AOP.

sections.title: AOP in Action — Logging Aspect
Key Points
sections.content:
- **AOP separates cross-cutting concerns** — logging, security, and transactions are written once in an aspect instead of being duplicated across every service method
- **Proxy-based interception** — Spring wraps beans in JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) or CGLIB proxies (class-based) to intercept method calls at runtime
- **Self-invocation bypasses AOP** — when a method calls another method in the same class, it skips the proxy, so advice won't trigger on the internal call
- **`@EnableAspectJAutoProxy` activates AOP** — Spring Boot auto-configures this with `spring-boot-starter-aop`, but non-Boot apps must add it to a `@Configuration` class
- **`@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Secured` all use AOP** — Spring's most popular declarative features are implemented as aspects under the hood

**AOP** stands for Aspect-Oriented Programming, and in Spring it's how you handle **cross-cutting concerns** — things like logging, security, and transactions that affect many parts of your application but don't belong in any single class.

The idea is simple: instead of copying logging code into every service method, you write it once in an **aspect** and declare where it should apply using a **pointcut expression**. Spring then wraps your beans in **proxies** that intercept method calls and run the aspect logic automatically. When you use `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, or `@Secured`, you're actually using AOP under the hood — Spring creates a proxy that adds the behavior around your method.

The key thing to know is that Spring AOP is **proxy-based**, which means it only works on method calls that go through the proxy. If a method calls another method in the same class (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed and the advice won't run. That's probably the most common gotcha with Spring AOP.

questions.title: AOP Terminology - Aspect, Advice, Pointcut, JoinPoint
questions.question: What are the key terms in AOP?

answer.summary: AOP terminology includes Aspect (modularized concern), Advice (action taken), Pointcut (where to apply), JoinPoint (execution point), and Weaving (linking aspects to targets).

sections.title: The Core AOP Vocabulary
sections.content:
Understanding AOP requires grasping five key terms that form its conceptual model. These terms map directly to how Spring AOP operates and how you write aspect code. Think of it like a movie production: the **Aspect** is the screenplay, the **Advice** is the specific scene, the **Pointcut** tells the director where to insert it, the **JoinPoint** is the exact frame, and **Weaving** is the editing process that stitches it all together.

Without a solid understanding of these terms, AOP configuration becomes confusing — you'll see annotations like `@Around`, `@Pointcut`, and parameters like `JoinPoint` but won't know how they connect. Let's break each one down.

sections.title: Aspect, Advice, and Pointcut
sections.content:
**Aspect** is a class that encapsulates a cross-cutting concern. In Spring, you annotate it with `@Aspect` and `@Component`. A single aspect can contain multiple pieces of advice. For example, a `SecurityAspect` might have one advice for authentication and another for authorization.

**Advice** is the actual action that an aspect performs at a particular point. There are five types:
- `@Before` — runs before the method
- `@After` — runs after the method (regardless of outcome)
- `@AfterReturning` — runs only if the method completes successfully
- `@AfterThrowing` — runs only if the method throws an exception
- `@Around` — wraps the method, runs before and after, can even skip the method entirely

**Pointcut** is a predicate expression that matches join points — it defines WHERE advice should be applied. You write it using AspectJ expression language: `execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))` matches all methods in the service package. Pointcuts can be combined with `&&`, `||`, and `!` operators for complex matching.

sections.title: JoinPoint, Target, and Weaving
sections.content:
**JoinPoint** represents a point during program execution — in Spring AOP, this is always a **method execution** (Spring AOP doesn't support field-level interception like full AspectJ). The `JoinPoint` parameter in your advice method gives you access to the method signature, arguments, and target object.

**Target object** is the actual object being advised — the real bean behind the proxy. You can access it via `joinPoint.getTarget()`. The **proxy object** is what callers interact with; it delegates to the target after running advice.

**Weaving** is the process of linking aspects with target objects to create advised objects. Spring AOP performs **runtime weaving** using proxies. This contrasts with compile-time weaving (AspectJ compiler) or load-time weaving (class loader instrumentation). Runtime weaving is simpler to set up but has the self-invocation limitation — when a method calls another method in the same class, it bypasses the proxy.

**Introduction** (also called inter-type declaration) allows you to declare additional methods or fields on advised objects. Spring AOP supports this via the `@DeclareParents` annotation, letting you make a bean implement a new interface at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Aspect = modularized concern** — a `@Aspect @Component` class that bundles related advice methods and pointcuts into a single reusable unit
- **Advice = the action at a specific timing** — `@Before`, `@After`, `@Around`, `@AfterReturning`, and `@AfterThrowing` define what happens and when relative to the target method
- **Pointcut = where to apply advice** — an AspectJ expression like `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` that selects which method executions to intercept
- **JoinPoint = the intercepted method execution** — gives access to `getSignature()`, `getArgs()`, and `getTarget()` inside advice methods
- **Weaving = linking aspects to targets** — Spring performs runtime weaving via proxies, unlike AspectJ which supports compile-time and load-time weaving

A **Pointcut** is the expression that selects which methods get intercepted — something like `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` to target all methods in your service package. The **JoinPoint** is the actual method execution being intercepted; your advice method receives a `JoinPoint` parameter that gives you access to the method name, arguments, and target object.

Finally, **Weaving** is the process of connecting aspects to target objects. Spring does this at **runtime** using proxies, which is simpler than AspectJ's compile-time or load-time weaving but has the self-invocation limitation.

questions.title: Aspect - Modularized Cross-Cutting Concern
questions.question: What is an Aspect in AOP?

answer.summary: An Aspect in AOP is a modularized cross-cutting concern — a class annotated with @Aspect that contains advice methods and pointcut definitions, applied across multiple components without modifying their code.

sections.title: Understanding the Aspect Concept
sections.content:
An **Aspect** is the fundamental building block of AOP — it's a regular Java class that encapsulates a cross-cutting concern into a single, reusable module. In Spring, you mark it with `@Aspect` (from AspectJ) and `@Component` (so Spring manages it as a bean).

The motivation is simple: without aspects, you'd scatter logging, security, or transaction code across dozens of service methods. An aspect lets you write that logic once and declare where it applies. It's the AOP equivalent of extracting a utility class, except the "calling" is done automatically by the framework rather than manually by the developer.

An aspect combines two things: **what to do** (advice methods like `@Before`, `@Around`) and **where to do it** (pointcut expressions). A single aspect class can contain multiple advice methods targeting different pointcuts, making it a cohesive module for one concern.

sections.title: Creating and Registering an Aspect
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Aspect` + `@Component` required** — `@Aspect` alone doesn't register the class as a Spring bean; you need `@Component` or explicit `@Bean` registration
- **Combines what and where** — an aspect contains advice methods (what to do) and pointcut expressions (where to apply), keeping a concern cohesive in one class
- **Singleton and stateless** — aspects are singleton beans by default; mutable state would cause thread-safety issues in concurrent environments
- **`@Order` controls execution sequence** — when multiple aspects apply to the same join point, `@Order(1)` runs before `@Order(2)`, giving you deterministic ordering
- **Named pointcuts for reuse** — define `@Pointcut` methods once and reference them across multiple advice methods to avoid duplicating expressions

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An **Aspect** is just a class that encapsulates a cross-cutting concern — like logging, auditing, or security — so you write the logic once instead of duplicating it across your codebase. In Spring, you mark it with `@Aspect` and `@Component`.

Inside the aspect, you define two things: **what to do** (advice methods like `@Before`, `@Around`) and **where to do it** (pointcut expressions). You can have multiple advice methods in a single aspect, and you can define reusable pointcuts with `@Pointcut` so you don't repeat the same expression everywhere.

A few practical things to know: aspects are **singleton beans** by default, so they should be stateless to avoid thread-safety issues. If you have multiple aspects, you can control execution order with `@Order`. And remember, `@Aspect` alone doesn't make it a Spring bean — you need `@Component` or a `@Bean` definition alongside it.

questions.title: AOP Advice Types - Before, After, Around, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing
questions.question: What are the different types of advice in AOP?

answer.summary: Spring AOP provides five advice types: @Before (runs before method), @After (runs after regardless), @AfterReturning (on success), @AfterThrowing (on exception), and @Around (wraps entire method execution).

sections.title: Five Types of Advice in Spring AOP
sections.content:
Advice defines **what action** an aspect takes and **when** it takes it relative to the target method execution. Spring AOP supports five advice types, each serving a different interception timing. Choosing the right advice type matters — using `@Around` for everything works but is overkill; using `@Before` when you need to modify the return value won't work at all.

The five types form a lifecycle around method execution: before the method runs, after it succeeds, after it throws, after it completes (either way), or wrapping the entire execution. Understanding when to use each one helps you write cleaner, more focused aspects.

sections.title: Before, After, and AfterReturning
AfterThrowing and Around
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Before` runs pre-method** — cannot prevent execution (unless it throws) or modify the return value; ideal for validation and logging entry
- **`@AfterReturning` captures the result** — binds the return value to a parameter for inspection, but only fires on successful completion
- **`@AfterThrowing` captures exceptions** — binds the thrown exception for logging/alerting but does not swallow it; the exception still propagates
- **`@After` is a finally block** — runs regardless of success or failure, useful for cleanup like releasing resources or stopping timers
- **`@Around` gives full control** — wraps the entire method via `ProceedingJoinPoint.proceed()`, letting you modify args, change return values, retry, or skip execution entirely

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring AOP has five advice types, and they map to different points around a method execution. **`@Before`** runs before the method — good for validation and logging. **`@AfterReturning`** runs only when the method succeeds, and you can bind the return value to inspect it. **`@AfterThrowing`** runs only when the method throws an exception. **`@After`** is like a `finally` block — runs regardless of outcome.

The most powerful is **`@Around`**, which wraps the entire method. You get a `ProceedingJoinPoint` and you must call `proceed()` to let the actual method run. This gives you full control — you can modify arguments, change the return value, handle exceptions, or even skip the method entirely. That's how Spring implements things like retry logic and performance monitoring.

The best practice is to use the **narrowest advice type** that fits your need. Don't use `@Around` for simple logging that only needs `@Before`. It keeps your aspects cleaner and less error-prone.

questions.title: Pointcut - Matching Join Points
questions.question: What is a Pointcut in AOP?

answer.summary: A Pointcut in AOP is a predicate expression that selects join points (method executions) where advice should be applied, using AspectJ expression language like execution(), within(), and @annotation().

sections.title: What Is a Pointcut
sections.content:
A **Pointcut** is a filter expression that tells Spring AOP **which methods** to intercept. Without pointcuts, an aspect would apply to every method in the application — pointcuts provide the precision to target exactly the methods you care about.

In Spring AOP, pointcuts are defined using the **AspectJ pointcut expression language**. The most commonly used designator is `execution()`, which matches method execution join points based on method signature patterns. You can also use `within()` to match by class, `@annotation()` to match by annotation, and `args()` to match by argument type.

Pointcuts can be **inline** (written directly in the advice annotation) or **named** (defined as a separate method with `@Pointcut` for reuse across multiple advice methods).

sections.title: Defining and Combining Pointcuts
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`execution()` is the primary designator** — matches method signatures with patterns like `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` for all methods in the service package
- **Named pointcuts promote reuse** — define `@Pointcut("expression")` on a method and reference it by name in multiple advice annotations
- **Combine with `&&`, `||`, `!`** — compose complex pointcuts from simple ones, e.g., `serviceLayer() && !readOperations()` for write-only service methods
- **`@annotation()` enables opt-in behavior** — match methods by their annotations like `@annotation(Loggable)`, letting developers explicitly mark methods for interception
- **`bean()` is Spring-specific** — match by bean name with wildcards like `bean(*Service)`, not available in standard AspectJ

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **Pointcut** is an expression that tells Spring AOP **which methods to intercept**. Without it, your advice would apply to every method in the application. The most common pointcut designator is `execution()`, which matches methods by their signature — like `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` for all methods in the service package.

You can also use `within()` for class-level matching, `@annotation()` to target methods with specific annotations, and `bean()` to match by bean name. These can be combined with `&&`, `||`, and `!` for complex filters. For example, `serviceLayer() && !readOperations()` would match only write operations in your service layer.

The practical tip is to **name your pointcuts** using `@Pointcut` on a method and then reference them by name in your advice. This makes the expressions reusable and much more readable than repeating long expressions inline.

questions.title: @Before Advice - Execute Before Method
questions.question: What is @Before advice?

answer.summary: @Before advice executes before the target method runs, commonly used for validation, logging, and security checks. It receives a JoinPoint parameter for accessing method metadata and arguments.

sections.title: How @Before Advice Works
sections.content:
The `@Before` advice is the simplest advice type in Spring AOP — it runs **immediately before** the target method executes. It's invoked after the proxy intercepts the call but before the actual bean method runs.

`@Before` advice cannot prevent the target method from executing (unless it throws an exception). It also cannot modify the method's return value. If you need either of those capabilities, use `@Around` instead. The strength of `@Before` lies in its simplicity — it's perfect for cross-cutting tasks that need to happen before a method, like logging entry points, validating preconditions, or recording audit trails.

The advice method receives a `JoinPoint` parameter that provides rich metadata: the method signature, the arguments passed, the target object, and the proxy object.

sections.title: @Before in Practice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Runs after proxy intercept, before target** — the advice method executes between the proxy receiving the call and the actual bean method running
- **`JoinPoint` provides method metadata** — access the method name via `getSignature()`, arguments via `getArgs()`, and the target bean via `getTarget()`
- **Cannot modify the return value** — `@Before` has no access to the method result; use `@Around` if you need to change what the caller receives
- **Throwing stops the target method** — if `@Before` advice throws an exception, the target method never executes and the exception propagates to the caller
- **Best for validation and audit logging** — check preconditions, verify permissions, or record method entry without affecting the method's output

questions.title: @Around Advice - Wrap Method Execution
questions.question: What is @Around advice?

answer.summary: @Around advice is the most powerful AOP advice type — it wraps the entire method execution, controlling whether the method runs, modifying arguments and return values, and handling exceptions.

sections.title: Understanding @Around Advice
@Around for Timing, Retries, and Caching
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Must call `proceed()` to execute the target** — forgetting this means the actual method never runs and the caller gets `null` or the advice's return value
- **`ProceedingJoinPoint` extends `JoinPoint`** — adds `proceed()` and `proceed(Object[] args)` for executing the target with original or modified arguments
- **Can modify arguments and return values** — pass a different `Object[]` to `proceed(args)` to change inputs, or transform the result before returning
- **Must declare `throws Throwable`** — the target method may throw checked exceptions that must propagate through the advice
- **Use sparingly — prefer narrower advice types** — `@Around` is powerful but adds complexity; use `@Before` or `@AfterReturning` when you don't need full control

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Around` is the most powerful advice type because it completely wraps the target method. Your advice method receives a **`ProceedingJoinPoint`** and you call `proceed()` to execute the actual method. Everything before `proceed()` runs pre-method, everything after runs post-method.

The key rules: you **must** call `proceed()` or the target method never runs. You **must** return the result (or a modified version). And you should declare `throws Throwable` because the target method might throw checked exceptions.

What makes `@Around` special is the control it gives you. You can modify the arguments by passing a different `Object[]` to `proceed(args)`. You can transform the return value before sending it back. You can catch exceptions and retry. You can even skip the target method entirely and return a cached value. That's why Spring uses `@Around` internally for things like `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, and retry logic.

questions.title: Pointcut Expressions - execution, within, args
questions.question: How do you write pointcut expressions?

answer.summary: Pointcut expressions use AspectJ syntax to select method join points. The execution() designator matches by method signature, while within(), @annotation(), args(), and bean() provide alternative matching strategies.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Pointcut Expression
sections.content:
Pointcut expressions are the targeting language of Spring AOP — they define precisely which methods get intercepted. Spring uses a subset of the **AspectJ pointcut expression language**, and mastering the syntax is essential for writing effective aspects.

The most important designator is `execution()`, which matches method signatures using a pattern:

```
execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws?)
```

Wildcards make patterns flexible: `*` matches any single element, `..` matches zero or more (packages or parameters), and `+` matches subclasses. For example, `execution(* com.example..*.*(..))` matches any method in any class under `com.example` with any number of parameters.

sections.title: Common Pointcut Patterns
Combining and Reusing Expressions
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`execution()` syntax: `return-type declaring-type.method-name(params)`** — wildcards `*` (any one) and `..` (any zero or more) make patterns flexible
- **`within()` simplifies package matching** — `within(com.example.service..*)` is more readable than the equivalent `execution()` pattern for class-level targeting
- **`@annotation()` for annotation-driven AOP** — matches methods annotated with a specific annotation, enabling developers to opt-in via markers like `@Loggable`
- **`args()` matches runtime argument types** — `args(String, ..)` matches methods whose first argument is a `String` at runtime, regardless of declared type
- **Combine and name pointcuts for maintainability** — `@Pointcut("serviceLayer() && writeOps()")` creates composable, self-documenting expressions that reduce duplication

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pointcut expressions use **AspectJ syntax** and the `execution()` designator is by far the most common. The pattern is `execution(return-type declaring-type.method-name(params))` where `*` matches any single element and `..` matches zero or more. So `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` means any return type, any class under the service package and sub-packages, any method name, any parameters.

Beyond `execution()`, you'll use `within()` for package-level matching (cleaner than the equivalent execution pattern), `@annotation()` to match methods with a specific annotation, `args()` for runtime argument types, and `bean()` to match by bean name with wildcards like `*Service`.

The practical advice: **name your pointcuts** with `@Pointcut` methods and compose them with `&&`, `||`, `!`. Something like `inServiceLayer() && writeOperations()` is much more readable than a giant inline expression. And always be specific — an overly broad pointcut like `execution(* *(..))` will proxy every bean and kill performance.

questions.title: ApplicationContext - Spring Container Interface
questions.question: What is ApplicationContext in Spring?

answer.summary: ApplicationContext is the central interface for Spring's IoC container. It manages bean lifecycle, dependency injection, event publishing, and resource loading, extending BeanFactory with enterprise-level features.

sections.title: ApplicationContext — The Spring Container
sections.content:
**ApplicationContext** is the heart of any Spring application — it's the IoC (Inversion of Control) container that manages the complete lifecycle of beans: creation, configuration, dependency injection, and destruction. When you start a Spring application, the first thing that happens is the creation of an `ApplicationContext`.

`ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory`, which provides basic bean management. On top of that, `ApplicationContext` adds enterprise features:
- **Automatic BeanPostProcessor registration** — post-processors are detected and applied without manual registration
- **Event publishing** — `ApplicationEventPublisher` for decoupled event-driven communication
- **Internationalization (i18n)** — `MessageSource` for resolving messages in different locales
- **Resource loading** — `ResourceLoader` for accessing files, URLs, and classpath resources
- **Environment abstraction** — access to properties and profiles

In practice, you almost always use `ApplicationContext` rather than `BeanFactory`. The only reason to use `BeanFactory` directly is in resource-constrained environments (like applets) where memory overhead matters and you don't need the enterprise features.

sections.title: Creating and Using ApplicationContext
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Central IoC container** — manages bean creation, dependency injection, lifecycle callbacks, and destruction for the entire application
- **Extends BeanFactory with enterprise features** — adds event publishing, i18n, resource loading, and automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration beyond basic bean management
- **Auto-detects and applies BeanPostProcessors** — unlike `BeanFactory`, `ApplicationContext` automatically finds and registers post-processors for `@Autowired`, AOP, etc.
- **Supports hierarchical contexts** — child contexts can access parent beans but not vice versa, enabling modular application architectures
- **Spring Boot auto-creates the right type** — `SpringApplication.run()` returns a `ConfigurableApplicationContext` specialized for servlet, reactive, or standalone use

It extends `BeanFactory` with enterprise features like **event publishing** (`ApplicationEventPublisher`), **i18n** (`MessageSource`), **resource loading**, and **automatic BeanPostProcessor registration**. That last one is why you'd almost always use `ApplicationContext` over plain `BeanFactory` — it automatically detects and applies post-processors that handle `@Autowired`, AOP proxies, and other annotations.

In Spring Boot, you rarely interact with `ApplicationContext` directly — `SpringApplication.run()` creates the right type automatically and dependency injection handles the rest. questions.title: ApplicationContext Types - ClassPath, FileSystem, Web
questions.question: What are the different types of ApplicationContext?

answer.summary: Spring provides several ApplicationContext implementations: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext for Java config, ClassPathXmlApplicationContext for XML on classpath, FileSystemXmlApplicationContext for XML on filesystem, and WebApplicationContext for web apps.

sections.title: Choosing the Right ApplicationContext
sections.content:
Spring offers multiple `ApplicationContext` implementations, each designed for a specific configuration style and deployment environment. Choosing the right one depends on whether you use Java-based or XML-based configuration, whether you're building a web application, and whether you're using Spring Boot.

The main implementations form two families: **standalone** contexts (for desktop apps, batch jobs, tests) and **web** contexts (for servlet-based web applications). Modern Spring applications predominantly use `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` or its web counterpart, but understanding the XML variants is still important for maintaining legacy codebases.

sections.title: ApplicationContext Implementations
sections.content:
| Implementation | Config Style | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` | Java `@Configuration` classes | Modern standalone apps, unit tests |
| `ClassPathXmlApplicationContext` | XML on classpath | Legacy apps, XML-configured projects |
| `FileSystemXmlApplicationContext` | XML on filesystem | External config files outside JAR |
| `AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext` | Java config for web | Modern Spring MVC / Spring Boot web apps |
| `XmlWebApplicationContext` | XML config for web | Legacy web applications |
| `GenericApplicationContext` | Programmatic registration | Advanced/custom container setup |

In Spring Boot, `SpringApplication.run()` automatically creates the appropriate context type:
- `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext` for servlet web apps
- `AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContext` for reactive (WebFlux) apps
- `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` for non-web apps

You can mix configuration styles — an `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` can import XML configurations via `@ImportResource`, and XML contexts can enable annotation scanning with `<context:component-scan>`.

sections.content:
- **`AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`** — bootstraps from `@Configuration` classes with type-safe Java config; the standard for modern standalone Spring apps
- **`ClassPathXmlApplicationContext`** — loads XML config from the classpath; still common in legacy codebases and used for backward compatibility
- **`FileSystemXmlApplicationContext`** — loads XML config from filesystem paths; useful when config lives outside the JAR/WAR
- **Web variants auto-register web-specific scopes** — `AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext` and `XmlWebApplicationContext` add request, session, and application scopes
- **Spring Boot auto-selects the context type** — servlet apps get `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext`, reactive apps get the reactive variant, non-web get plain `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`

For web apps, there are web-specific variants: `AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext` and `XmlWebApplicationContext`, which add web scopes like request and session.

questions.title: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext - Java Config Context
questions.question: What is AnnotationConfigApplicationContext?

answer.summary: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext is a standalone Spring container that accepts @Configuration classes and @Component-scanned classes as input, replacing XML-based configuration with type-safe Java code.

sections.title: Java-Based Container Configuration
sections.content:
`AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` is the modern way to bootstrap a Spring IoC container using Java-based configuration. Instead of XML files, you provide `@Configuration` classes that define beans using `@Bean` methods, and Spring scans for `@Component`-annotated classes.

This approach offers significant advantages over XML: **compile-time type safety** (typos in class names are caught by the compiler), **IDE support** (refactoring, navigation, autocomplete), and **programmatic logic** (you can use conditionals, loops, and method calls in bean definitions).

The context can be initialized with one or more `@Configuration` classes, and additional classes can be registered after construction using `register()`. You can also enable component scanning programmatically with `scan()`.

sections.title: Using AnnotationConfigApplicationContext
Key Points
sections.content:

questions.title: ApplicationContext getBean() - Retrieving Beans
questions.question: How do you retrieve beans from ApplicationContext?

answer.summary: ApplicationContext provides getBean() methods to retrieve beans by type, name, or both. Type-safe retrieval with getBean(Class<T>) is preferred; getBean(String) returns Object and requires casting.

sections.title: Retrieving Beans from the Container
sections.content:
While Spring's dependency injection means you rarely need to manually retrieve beans, understanding `getBean()` is important for bootstrap code, tests, integration with non-Spring code, and debugging. `ApplicationContext` inherits multiple `getBean()` overloads from `BeanFactory`.

The most important variants are:
- `getBean(Class<T> type)` — retrieves by type, throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` if multiple beans of that type exist
- `getBean(String name)` — retrieves by bean name, returns `Object` (requires casting)
- `getBean(String name, Class<T> type)` — retrieves by name with type safety
- `getBean(Class<T> type, Object... args)` — retrieves a prototype bean with constructor arguments

In production code, prefer **constructor injection** over `getBean()`. Manual retrieval couples your code to the Spring API and makes testing harder.

sections.content:

- **`getBean(String)` returns Object** — retrieves by bean name but requires explicit casting; less safe but useful when the name is known dynamically
- **`getBeansOfType(Class<T>)` returns all matching beans** — returns `Map<String, T>` of all beans assignable to the type; useful for strategy patterns and plugin architectures
- **Prefer dependency injection over `getBean()`** — manual retrieval couples code to the Spring API and makes unit testing harder; use only in bootstrap or integration code
- **`containsBean()` checks existence safely** — avoids `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` by letting you verify a bean exists before attempting retrieval

If you need a specific named bean, use `getBean("myBean", UserService.class)` for both name and type safety.

questions.title: Spring Application Events - Event Publishing
questions.question: How does event publishing work in Spring?

answer.summary: Spring's event publishing mechanism enables loose coupling between components. ApplicationContext acts as an event publisher; beans can publish events via ApplicationEventPublisher and listen via @EventListener or ApplicationListener.

sections.title: Event-Driven Architecture in Spring
sections.content:
Spring's event mechanism provides a publish-subscribe model that lets beans communicate without direct references to each other. This promotes **loose coupling** — the publisher doesn't need to know who's listening, and listeners don't need to know who's publishing.

The system has three parts:
1. **Event** — any object (since Spring 4.2, no need to extend `ApplicationEvent`)
2. **Publisher** — injects `ApplicationEventPublisher` and calls `publishEvent()`
3. **Listener** — a method annotated with `@EventListener` or a class implementing `ApplicationListener`

Spring also publishes its own lifecycle events: `ContextRefreshedEvent` (context initialized), `ContextStartedEvent`, `ContextStoppedEvent`, and `ContextClosedEvent`. You can listen to these to perform initialization or cleanup tasks.

sections.content:
- **Publish-subscribe model for loose coupling** — publishers call `publishEvent()` without knowing who listens; listeners handle events without knowing who publishes
- **Events are plain POJOs since Spring 4.2** — no need to extend `ApplicationEvent`; any object can be published and received based on its type
- **Synchronous by default** — listeners run in the publisher's thread; add `@Async` on the listener and `@EnableAsync` on config for non-blocking processing
- **Spring publishes lifecycle events** — `ContextRefreshedEvent`, `ContextClosedEvent`, `ContextStartedEvent`, and `ContextStoppedEvent` let you hook into container lifecycle
- **`@Order` controls listener execution sequence** — when multiple listeners handle the same event type, `@Order(1)` runs before `@Order(2)`

questions.title: ApplicationEvent and ApplicationListener - Event Handling
questions.question: What are ApplicationEvent and ApplicationListener?

answer.summary: ApplicationEvent is the base class for Spring events, and ApplicationListener is the interface for handling them. Since Spring 4.2, events don't need to extend ApplicationEvent and listeners can use @EventListener instead.

sections.title: The Traditional Event Model
sections.content:
Before Spring 4.2, the event system required two specific types: events had to extend `ApplicationEvent`, and listeners had to implement `ApplicationListener<E>`. While this still works and is fully supported, the modern approach using plain POJOs and `@EventListener` is simpler.

`ApplicationEvent` extends `java.util.EventObject` and carries a timestamp and a source reference (the object that published the event). `ApplicationListener<E>` is a functional interface with a single method `onApplicationEvent(E event)` that gets called when a matching event is published.

The typed generic parameter `ApplicationListener<OrderEvent>` tells Spring to only deliver `OrderEvent` instances to this listener — you get automatic type filtering without any conditional logic.

- **Plain POJOs replace both since Spring 4.2** — events don't need a base class and listeners can use `@EventListener` methods instead of implementing the interface
- **Traditional model still used for Spring internals** — `ContextRefreshedEvent`, `ContextClosedEvent`, and other framework events extend `ApplicationEvent`
- **`@EventListener` methods can return events** — returning an object from a listener auto-publishes it, enabling event chaining without injecting `ApplicationEventPublisher`

questions.title: @EventListener Annotation - Simplified Event Handling
questions.question: What is @EventListener annotation?

answer.summary: @EventListener is a method-level annotation that simplifies event handling — no need to implement ApplicationListener or extend ApplicationEvent. It supports conditional filtering, async execution, and event chaining.

sections.title: Simplified Event Handling with @EventListener
sections.content:
The `@EventListener` annotation, introduced in Spring 4.2, lets any `@Component` method handle events without implementing `ApplicationListener`. The method parameter type determines which events it receives — Spring automatically filters and delivers only matching events.

This annotation-based approach is superior to the interface approach for several reasons:
- **No boilerplate** — no interface to implement, no generic type parameter
- **Multiple handlers per class** — one component can have many `@EventListener` methods for different events
- **Conditional filtering** — use SpEL expressions to filter events beyond type matching
- **Event chaining** — return an event from a listener to trigger another event
- **Async support** — combine with `@Async` for non-blocking event processing

sections.title: @EventListener Features

sections.content:
- **Method parameter type determines event filtering** — Spring delivers only events matching the parameter type; no need for `instanceof` checks or interface generics
- **`condition` attribute uses SpEL for fine-grained filtering** — `@EventListener(condition = "#event.amount > 1000")` filters events beyond type matching
- **Returning an object publishes a new event** — enables event chaining without injecting `ApplicationEventPublisher` into the listener class
- **Multiple listeners per class** — one `@Component` can have several `@EventListener` methods for different event types, unlike the interface approach which is one per class
- **Combine with `@Async` for non-blocking processing** — requires `@EnableAsync` on a `@Configuration` class and an `Executor` bean for thread management

sections.content:

It has some powerful features: `condition` takes a SpEL expression for filtering beyond type (`@EventListener(condition = "#event.amount > 1000")`), returning an object from a listener **auto-publishes it** as a new event (event chaining), and you can have **multiple listener methods** in one class for different event types.

For async processing, combine `@EventListener` with `@Async` and enable `@EnableAsync`. Important to know: synchronous listeners run in the publisher's thread — if the listener throws an exception, it propagates to the publisher. questions.title: Spring Environment Abstraction - Properties and Profiles
questions.question: What is Environment abstraction in Spring?

answer.summary: Spring's Environment abstraction unifies access to properties (from files, env vars, system props) and profiles (dev, test, prod). It provides getProperty() for values and @Profile for conditional bean registration.

sections.title: Properties and Profiles in Spring
sections.content:
The **Environment** abstraction in Spring serves two purposes: it provides a unified API for **property resolution** (reading configuration values from multiple sources) and **profile management** (activating different configurations for different deployment environments).

For properties, `Environment` searches through an ordered list of `PropertySource` objects: system properties, environment variables, `application.properties`, JNDI attributes, and more. You can access any property via `env.getProperty("key")` or the convenient `@Value("${key}")` annotation. Property sources have a defined precedence — system properties override application.properties, command-line arguments override both.

For profiles, `Environment` tracks which profiles are active and determines which `@Profile`-annotated beans should be created. A common pattern is defining `dev`, `test`, and `prod` profiles with different database configurations, logging levels, and feature flags.

sections.title: Working with Environment
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unified property resolution** — reads from `application.properties`, system properties, environment variables, and JNDI in a defined precedence order
- **`@Value("${key:default}")` injects properties** — Spring resolves placeholders at injection time; the default value after `:` prevents failures when a property is missing
- **Profiles activate conditional beans** — `@Profile("dev")` beans are only created when the `dev` profile is active, enabling environment-specific configuration
- **Multiple profile activation methods** — set via `spring.profiles.active` in properties, `--spring.profiles.active` on command line, or `setActiveProfiles()` programmatically
- **Property source precedence matters** — command-line args override `application.properties`, which overrides `application-{profile}.properties`; know the order to debug config issues

For properties, you can inject `Environment` and call `getProperty("key")`, or use the more convenient `@Value("${key:default}")` annotation. Property sources have a defined precedence — command-line arguments beat `application.properties`, which beats profile-specific files.

For profiles, you annotate beans with `@Profile("dev")` or `@Profile("prod")` and Spring only creates them when the matching profile is active. questions.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle - Creation to Destruction
questions.question: What is the lifecycle of a Spring bean?

answer.summary: A Spring bean's lifecycle includes instantiation, dependency injection, initialization callbacks (@PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, custom init), use, and destruction callbacks (@PreDestroy, destroy, custom destroy).

sections.title: The Complete Bean Lifecycle
sections.content:
Every Spring bean goes through a well-defined lifecycle managed by the IoC container. Understanding this lifecycle is crucial for initializing resources (database connections, thread pools), validating configuration after injection, and cleaning up resources on shutdown.

The lifecycle has these phases in order:
1. **Instantiation** — Spring creates the bean instance (via constructor)
2. **Dependency Injection** — Spring injects dependencies (via setters or fields)
3. **Aware callbacks** — Spring calls `BeanNameAware.setBeanName()`, `ApplicationContextAware.setApplicationContext()`, etc.
4. **BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization()** — pre-init hook for all beans
5. **Initialization** — `@PostConstruct` → `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` → custom `init-method`
6. **BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization()** — post-init hook (AOP proxies are created here)
7. **Bean is ready for use**
8. **Destruction** — `@PreDestroy` → `DisposableBean.destroy()` → custom `destroy-method`

sections.title: Why Lifecycle Order Matters
sections.content:
The order of initialization callbacks is critical. A common mistake is trying to use injected dependencies in the constructor — at that point, setter-injected or field-injected dependencies haven't been set yet. That's why `@PostConstruct` exists: it runs **after** all dependencies are injected.

The three initialization mechanisms have a defined priority:
1. `@PostConstruct` (JSR-250) — runs first, most commonly used
2. `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` — runs second, couples code to Spring API
3. Custom init method (via `@Bean(initMethod="init")`) — runs third, no Spring dependency

The same priority applies in reverse for destruction:
1. `@PreDestroy` → 2. `DisposableBean.destroy()` → 3. Custom destroy method

**Important**: Prototype-scoped beans do NOT get destruction callbacks. Spring creates them and hands them off — it doesn't track their lifecycle after that. Only singleton beans get proper destruction.

BeanPostProcessors are especially important because they're how Spring implements many features internally. `@Autowired` processing, `@Value` resolution, AOP proxy creation, and `@Scheduled` setup all happen through BeanPostProcessors.

sections.content:
- **Instantiation → DI → Init → Use → Destroy** — the five phases every singleton bean goes through, managed entirely by the Spring container
- **`@PostConstruct` runs after all injection** — the safe place to use injected dependencies for initialization; constructors run before setter/field injection completes
- **BeanPostProcessors wrap each bean** — `postProcessBeforeInitialization` runs before `@PostConstruct`, `postProcessAfterInitialization` after (AOP proxies are created here)
- **Three init mechanisms in fixed order** — `@PostConstruct` → `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` → custom `init-method`, each running in sequence if present
- **Prototype beans skip destruction** — Spring does not track prototypes after creation; `@PreDestroy` callbacks are never called, so the client must handle cleanup

questions.title: Bean Lifecycle Callbacks - Init and Destroy Methods
questions.question: How do you define initialization and destruction callbacks for beans?

answer.summary: Spring provides three ways to define init/destroy callbacks: @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy annotations, InitializingBean/DisposableBean interfaces, and custom methods via @Bean(initMethod, destroyMethod).

sections.title: Three Mechanisms for Lifecycle Callbacks
sections.content:
Spring supports three approaches for hooking into bean initialization and destruction, each with different trade-offs between convenience, coupling, and flexibility.

1. **JSR-250 Annotations** (`@PostConstruct`, `@PreDestroy`) — the recommended approach. Clean, standard Java annotations with no Spring dependency in your code.
2. **Spring Interfaces** (`InitializingBean`, `DisposableBean`) — tightly couples your bean to Spring's API but provides a clear contract.
3. **Custom Methods** (specified via `@Bean(initMethod="init", destroyMethod="cleanup")`) — zero coupling, useful for third-party classes you can't annotate.

You can mix all three on the same bean — Spring calls them in a defined order: `@PostConstruct` first, then `afterPropertiesSet()`, then the custom init method. The same order applies in reverse for destruction.

Key Points
sections.content:
- **JSR-250 annotations are the recommended approach** — `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` are standard Java, keeping your code framework-agnostic
- **Three callback mechanisms can coexist** — if all three are present on one bean, Spring calls them in order: annotation → interface → custom method
- **Custom init/destroy methods work with third-party classes** — `@Bean(initMethod="init", destroyMethod="close")` configures lifecycle for classes you can't annotate
- **`DisposableBean.destroy()` declares checked exceptions** — unlike `@PreDestroy` which cannot throw checked exceptions, the interface method allows `throws Exception`
- **Only singleton beans get destroy callbacks** — prototype-scoped beans are not tracked by the container after creation, so their destruction methods are never invoked

And **custom methods** via `@Bean(initMethod="init", destroyMethod="close")` have zero coupling, making them perfect for third-party classes you can't annotate.

If all three are present on one bean, Spring calls them in a fixed order: `@PostConstruct` first, then `afterPropertiesSet()`, then the custom init method. Same order reversed for destruction.

questions.title: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy - JSR-250 Annotations
questions.question: What are @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy annotations?

answer.summary: @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection to perform initialization; @PreDestroy runs before bean destruction for cleanup. They are JSR-250 standard annotations, not Spring-specific.

sections.title: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy Explained
sections.content:
`@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` are **JSR-250** (Java standard) annotations for lifecycle callbacks. They're the recommended way to perform initialization and cleanup in Spring beans because they don't couple your code to Spring's API.

`@PostConstruct` marks a method that should be called **once** immediately after the bean's dependencies have been injected. This is the right place to validate configuration, open connections, pre-load caches, or start background tasks. It solves the problem of needing to run initialization logic that depends on injected values — you can't do this in the constructor because field/setter injection hasn't happened yet.

`@PreDestroy` marks a method called **just before** the bean is removed from the container (during context shutdown). Use it for releasing resources like database connections, stopping executors, or flushing buffers. Note: `@PreDestroy` is NOT called for prototype-scoped beans — Spring doesn't manage their destruction.

sections.title: Practical Usage Patterns
Key Points
sections.content:
- **JSR-250 standard, not Spring-specific** — these annotations work in any compliant container (Java EE, Jakarta EE), making your code portable across frameworks
- **`@PostConstruct` fires after all dependency injection** — safe to use `@Autowired` fields and `@Value` properties that aren't available in the constructor
- **`@PreDestroy` fires before container shutdown** — use it to close connections, stop threads, flush buffers, or release external resources
- **Methods must be void, no-arg, non-static** — Spring ignores methods that don't match this signature; only one method per annotation per class is supported
- **Jakarta namespace in Spring Boot 3+** — import `jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct` instead of `javax.annotation.PostConstruct` after the Jakarta EE 9 migration

questions.title: InitializingBean and DisposableBean - Lifecycle Interfaces
questions.question: What are InitializingBean and DisposableBean interfaces?

answer.summary: InitializingBean and DisposableBean are Spring interfaces providing afterPropertiesSet() and destroy() lifecycle callbacks. They work but couple your code to Spring — prefer @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy instead.

sections.title: Interface-Based Lifecycle Callbacks
sections.content:
`InitializingBean` and `DisposableBean` are Spring framework interfaces that provide lifecycle callback methods. When a bean implements `InitializingBean`, Spring calls its `afterPropertiesSet()` method after dependency injection is complete. When a bean implements `DisposableBean`, Spring calls its `destroy()` method during container shutdown.

These interfaces predate the JSR-250 annotations and are functionally equivalent to `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy`. The key difference is **coupling**: implementing these interfaces makes your class directly dependent on the Spring framework, which violates the principle of framework-agnostic code.

The Spring team recommends `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` over these interfaces for your own classes. However, `InitializingBean` is used extensively in Spring's own internal code — classes like `JdbcTemplate`, `AbstractApplicationContext`, and `ProxyFactoryBean` all implement it. You'll also see it in older codebases that predate widespread annotation adoption.

- **`afterPropertiesSet()` runs after DI completes** — equivalent to `@PostConstruct` but couples your code to Spring's `InitializingBean` interface
- **`destroy()` runs on container shutdown** — equivalent to `@PreDestroy` but only for singletons; prototypes don't get destruction callbacks
- **Spring's internal classes use these interfaces** — `JdbcTemplate`, `AbstractApplicationContext`, and many framework classes implement `InitializingBean`
- **Fixed method names reduce flexibility** — you must name your methods `afterPropertiesSet` and `destroy`, unlike `@PostConstruct` which works on any method name
- **Can throw checked exceptions** — the interface methods declare `throws Exception`, giving them an advantage over `@PostConstruct` which cannot throw checked exceptions

questions.title: BeanPostProcessor - Custom Bean Processing
questions.question: What is BeanPostProcessor?

answer.summary: BeanPostProcessor is a Spring extension point that lets you modify or wrap bean instances before and after initialization. Spring uses it internally for @Autowired, AOP proxies, @Scheduled, and @Async processing.

sections.title: How BeanPostProcessor Works
sections.content:
`BeanPostProcessor` is one of Spring's most powerful extension points — it lets you intercept and modify **every bean** in the container during its initialization. It defines two callback methods:

1. `postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName)` — called after dependency injection but **before** `@PostConstruct` and `afterPropertiesSet()`
2. `postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName)` — called **after** all initialization callbacks complete

Both methods receive the bean instance and can return either the original bean or a **replacement** (often a proxy). This is how Spring implements many of its core features:
- `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` — processes `@Autowired` and `@Value` annotations
- `AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator` — creates AOP proxies for `@Aspect`-advised beans
- `ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` — registers `@Scheduled` methods
- `AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` — wraps `@Async` methods in executor-backed proxies

A `BeanPostProcessor` applies to all beans in the container — it acts as a global interceptor for bean initialization. This is why custom `BeanPostProcessor` implementations should be efficient and careful about which beans they modify.

- **Intercepts every bean during initialization** — `postProcessBeforeInitialization` and `postProcessAfterInitialization` run for all beans in the container
- **Powers Spring's core features** — `@Autowired` injection, `@Value` resolution, AOP proxying, `@Scheduled` registration, and `@Async` wrapping all use BeanPostProcessors
- **Can replace the bean with a proxy** — returning a different object from `postProcessAfterInitialization` swaps the original bean with a wrapper (how AOP works)
- **Created before regular beans** — BeanPostProcessors are instantiated early so they're ready to process other beans; their own dependencies skip some post-processing
- **Must always return the bean** — returning `null` removes the bean from the container; always return the original bean unless you intentionally want to replace it

questions.title: BeanFactoryPostProcessor - Modify Bean Definitions
questions.question: What is BeanFactoryPostProcessor?

answer.summary: BeanFactoryPostProcessor modifies bean definitions (metadata) before any beans are instantiated. It operates on the configuration level — changing class types, property values, and scope — not on bean instances.

sections.title: Modifying Bean Definitions Before Instantiation
sections.content:
`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` operates at a different level than `BeanPostProcessor`. While `BeanPostProcessor` works with **bean instances** (after creation), `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` works with **bean definitions** (the metadata/blueprint) **before** any beans are created.

This means a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` can:
- Change a bean's class type
- Modify property values in the definition
- Change scope from singleton to prototype
- Add or remove bean definitions entirely
- Resolve property placeholders (like `${db.url}`)

Spring's own `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` — it scans all bean definitions for `${...}` placeholders and replaces them with actual property values before beans are created. `ConfigurationClassPostProcessor` is another critical one — it processes `@Configuration` classes and registers the `@Bean` methods as bean definitions.

sections.title: Custom BeanFactoryPostProcessor
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Operates on bean definitions, not instances** — modifies metadata (class, scope, properties) before any beans are instantiated, unlike BeanPostProcessor which works on instances

- **Runs once at container startup** — receives the entire `ConfigurableListableBeanFactory` and can iterate over all bean definitions in a single method call
- **Should not instantiate beans** — calling `getBean()` inside a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` causes premature instantiation that bypasses other post-processors
- **`ConfigurationClassPostProcessor` processes `@Configuration`** — the most critical BFPP in Spring; it parses `@Configuration` classes and registers `@Bean` definitions

questions.title: Spring Aware Interfaces - ApplicationContextAware, BeanNameAware
questions.question: What are Aware interfaces in Spring?

answer.summary: Spring Aware interfaces (ApplicationContextAware, BeanNameAware, EnvironmentAware, etc.) let beans receive infrastructure references from the container, but they couple your code to Spring — prefer injection instead.

sections.title: Accessing Container Infrastructure
sections.content:
**Aware interfaces** are callback interfaces that let Spring beans access container infrastructure objects. When a bean implements an Aware interface, Spring calls the corresponding setter method during initialization, injecting the requested infrastructure reference.

The most commonly used Aware interfaces are:
- `ApplicationContextAware` — receives the `ApplicationContext` reference
- `BeanNameAware` — receives the bean's name as registered in the container
- `BeanFactoryAware` — receives the `BeanFactory` reference
- `EnvironmentAware` — receives the `Environment` object for property access
- `ResourceLoaderAware` — receives the `ResourceLoader` for loading files
- `ApplicationEventPublisherAware` — receives the event publisher
- `MessageSourceAware` — receives the `MessageSource` for i18n

However, in modern Spring code, **you rarely need Aware interfaces** because you can inject these objects directly via `@Autowired`. The only advantage of Aware interfaces is that they work even in scenarios where annotation-based injection isn't available (like in `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations).

sections.title: Aware Interfaces vs Direct Injection
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Receive container infrastructure references** — `ApplicationContextAware`, `BeanNameAware`, `EnvironmentAware` inject container objects via callback setters
- **Prefer direct injection in modern code** — `@Autowired ApplicationContext ctx` achieves the same result without coupling to Spring's Aware interfaces
- **`BeanNameAware.setBeanName()` runs first** — it's called before other Aware callbacks, giving the bean access to its registered name for logging or debugging
- **All Aware callbacks run before `@PostConstruct`** — the container infrastructure is available before initialization callbacks, ensuring post-construct methods can use them
- **Necessary in `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`** — Aware interfaces work in contexts where annotation-based injection isn't available, like very-early-stage bean processing

The main exception is inside `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations, where annotation-based injection isn't available.

All Aware callbacks run after dependency injection but before `@PostConstruct`, so by the time your init method runs, all infrastructure references are available. The callback order is defined: `BeanNameAware` first, then `BeanFactoryAware`, then `ApplicationContextAware`, and others in between.

questions.title: @Lazy Annotation - Delayed Bean Creation
questions.question: What is @Lazy annotation?

answer.summary: @Lazy delays bean creation from context startup to first access. It reduces startup time but moves initialization errors from startup to runtime, making them harder to catch early.

sections.title: Eager vs Lazy Bean Initialization
sections.content:
By default, Spring creates all singleton beans **eagerly** during `ApplicationContext` startup. This means every singleton is instantiated, injected, and initialized before the application is ready to serve requests. While this catches configuration errors early (fail-fast), it can slow down startup for large applications with hundreds of beans.

`@Lazy` tells Spring to **defer** bean creation until the bean is first requested — either via `getBean()`, dependency injection into another bean, or through a proxy. This can significantly reduce startup time when some beans are expensive to create (e.g., they open database connections, load large caches, or connect to external services) and may not be needed immediately.

The trade-off is clear: **lazy initialization moves errors from startup to runtime**. A misconfigured lazy bean won't fail until someone actually uses it, which could be hours after deployment. This is why Spring Boot's `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` (which makes ALL beans lazy) should be used cautiously in production.

sections.title: Using @Lazy Effectively
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Defers bean creation to first access** — the bean's constructor and `@PostConstruct` don't run at startup; they run when someone first calls a method on the bean
- **Trades startup speed for runtime risk** — lazy beans with configuration errors won't fail at deploy time; the error surfaces when the bean is first used
- **Useful for breaking circular dependencies** — `@Lazy` on one injection point injects a proxy, deferring the real bean's creation and breaking the construction-time cycle
- **`spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` makes all beans lazy** — a Spring Boot property for development speed; use `@Lazy(false)` to force eager loading of critical beans
- **Proxy-based when injected into eager beans** — `@Lazy` on a constructor parameter injects a CGLIB proxy that triggers real bean creation on first method call

questions.title: Spring Bean Scopes - Lifecycle and Availability
questions.question: What are bean scopes in Spring?

answer.summary: Spring bean scopes define how many instances the container creates and how long they live. The five built-in scopes are singleton (one per context), prototype (new each time), request, session, and application (web-only).

sections.title: Understanding Bean Scopes
sections.content:
A bean's **scope** determines two things: **how many instances** of that bean exist and **how long** each instance lives. Choosing the right scope is critical for correctness — using singleton scope for a bean that holds user-specific state causes data leakage between users; using prototype scope for a stateless service wastes memory creating unnecessary instances.

Spring provides five built-in scopes:

| Scope | Instances | Lifetime | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **singleton** (default) | One per ApplicationContext | Entire application | Stateless services, repositories, utilities |
| **prototype** | New instance every time | Until garbage collected | Stateful objects, command objects, non-thread-safe components |
| **request** | One per HTTP request | Single HTTP request | Request-scoped data, form objects |
| **session** | One per HTTP session | User session duration | Shopping cart, user preferences |
| **application** | One per ServletContext | Entire web app | Shared web-app state |

The first two (singleton and prototype) work in any Spring application. The last three (request, session, application) are available only in web-aware contexts like Spring MVC or Spring WebFlux.

sections.title: Singleton vs Prototype — The Key Decision
sections.content:
**Singleton** is the default and most common scope. Spring creates exactly one instance and caches it — every injection point and `getBean()` call returns the same object. This works perfectly for stateless services that process requests using only method parameters and local variables.

The critical rule for singletons: **they must be thread-safe**. In a web application, multiple threads (handling different HTTP requests) will access the same singleton instance concurrently. If a singleton has mutable instance fields, you'll get race conditions. The fix is simple: don't store request-specific state in instance fields.

**Prototype** scope creates a new instance every time the bean is requested. Spring creates it, injects dependencies, calls `@PostConstruct`, and hands it off — after that, Spring does NOT manage it (no `@PreDestroy` callback). This is appropriate for stateful objects that shouldn't be shared, like a builder pattern object or a non-thread-safe parser.

A common pitfall: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton gives you ONE prototype instance that lives forever (effectively becoming a singleton). To get a fresh prototype each time, use `ObjectFactory<T>`, `Provider<T>`, or `@Lookup` method injection.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton is the default** — Spring creates one instance per `ApplicationContext` and reuses it for every injection point; appropriate for stateless services
- **Prototype creates a new instance each time** — no caching, no `@PreDestroy` callback; the client is responsible for the bean's full lifecycle after creation
- **Request, session, and application are web-only** — available only in web-aware contexts; tied to HTTP request, HTTP session, and `ServletContext` lifecycles respectively
- **Scope mismatch requires scoped proxies** — injecting a shorter-lived bean (request) into a longer-lived one (singleton) needs `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`
- **Choose based on statefulness** — stateless → singleton, per-use state → prototype, per-request state → request scope, per-user state → session scope

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Bean scope controls **how many instances** Spring creates and **how long** they live. The default is **singleton** — one instance per ApplicationContext, shared everywhere. **Prototype** creates a new instance each time. Then there are three web-only scopes: **request** (one per HTTP request), **session** (one per user session), and **application** (one per ServletContext).

The key decision is about **statefulness**. Stateless services, repositories, and controllers should be singletons — there's no reason to create multiple identical instances. Stateful objects that carry per-use data (shopping carts, command objects) need prototype or a web scope.

The most common gotcha is **scope mismatch**: injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton. Since the singleton is created at startup (no request exists), you need a **scoped proxy** (`proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`) that delegates to the correct request-scoped instance at runtime.

questions.title: Singleton Scope - Single Bean Instance
questions.question: What is singleton scope?

answer.summary: Singleton scope (the default) means Spring creates exactly one bean instance per ApplicationContext and caches it. All injection points share the same object, making thread safety essential for mutable state.

sections.title: How Singleton Scope Works
sections.content:
When you define a bean without specifying a scope, Spring uses **singleton** scope by default. This means the container creates exactly **one instance** of the bean during initialization and returns that same instance for every subsequent request — whether via `@Autowired`, `getBean()`, or any other means.

The singleton instance is stored in the singleton cache (a `ConcurrentHashMap` inside `DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry`). It's created eagerly at startup (unless `@Lazy`) and destroyed when the `ApplicationContext` closes.

Important distinction: **Spring singleton ≠ GoF Singleton pattern**. The GoF Singleton guarantees one instance per JVM (using a private constructor and static instance). Spring singleton guarantees one instance **per ApplicationContext** — if you create two `ApplicationContext` instances, you get two "singleton" beans. Also, nothing prevents you from creating additional instances with `new` outside of Spring.

sections.title: Singleton Behavior and Thread Safety
Key Points
sections.content:
- **One instance per ApplicationContext** — not per JVM like the GoF Singleton pattern; creating two contexts produces two separate "singleton" beans
- **Eagerly created at startup** — unless `@Lazy` is applied; early creation catches configuration errors before the application serves traffic
- **Must be thread-safe** — multiple threads (HTTP requests) share the same instance concurrently; use `final` fields and avoid mutable shared state
- **Cached in `DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry`** — stored in a `ConcurrentHashMap`; every `getBean()` and `@Autowired` returns the exact same object reference
- **`@PreDestroy` called on context close** — destruction callbacks fire when `ApplicationContext.close()` is called, enabling proper resource cleanup

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Singleton** is Spring's default scope — the container creates **one instance** and returns it for every `@Autowired` injection and `getBean()` call. It's stored in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and lives for the entire application lifetime.

The most important rule: singleton beans **must be thread-safe**. In a web app, multiple threads handle concurrent requests using the same singleton instance. If you have mutable instance fields, you'll get race conditions. The fix: use `final` fields with constructor injection, keep beans stateless, and use `AtomicInteger` or `ConcurrentHashMap` if you genuinely need shared mutable state.

One common misconception: Spring singleton is **not** the GoF Singleton pattern. GoF Singleton guarantees one instance per JVM (private constructor, static field). Spring singleton guarantees one per ApplicationContext — you can have multiple contexts, and nothing stops you from calling `new` outside of Spring.

questions.title: Prototype Scope - New Bean Instance Per Request
questions.question: What is prototype scope?

answer.summary: Prototype scope creates a new bean instance every time it's requested from the container. Spring does not manage prototype beans after creation — no caching, no @PreDestroy callback, no lifecycle tracking.

sections.title: A New Instance Every Time
sections.content:
**Prototype scope** tells Spring to create a **brand new instance** every time the bean is requested — via `getBean()`, injection into another bean, or through a lookup method. Unlike singletons, Spring does not cache prototype beans; it creates them, injects dependencies, calls `@PostConstruct`, and then forgets about them.

This "fire and forget" behavior has an important consequence: **Spring does NOT call `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans**. The client code that receives the prototype instance is responsible for cleaning up resources. If a prototype bean holds a database connection, you must close it yourself.

Prototype scope is appropriate when each consumer needs its own isolated state — form objects, command objects, builder patterns, or any stateful component that shouldn't be shared between threads or request handlers.

questions.title: Singleton vs Prototype Scope - Scope Comparison
questions.question: What is the difference between singleton and prototype scope?

answer.summary: Singleton creates one shared instance (default, thread-safe requirement); prototype creates a new instance per request (no caching, no destroy callback). Choose based on statefulness and thread safety needs.

sections.title: When to Use Each Scope
sections.content:
The choice between singleton and prototype scope comes down to one question: **does this bean hold mutable state that shouldn't be shared?**

If the bean is stateless (like a service, repository, or utility), use **singleton** — there's no benefit to creating multiple identical instances. If the bean carries per-use state (like a shopping cart, form data, or a builder), use **prototype** — sharing it between callers would corrupt the state.

Most Spring applications are 95%+ singleton beans. Prototype scope is used sparingly for specific patterns where isolation is required.

sections.title: Singleton vs Prototype Comparison
sections.content:
| Characteristic | Singleton | Prototype |
|---|---|---|
| **Instances** | One per ApplicationContext | New per request |
| **Default?** | Yes | No — requires `@Scope("prototype")` |
| **Creation timing** | Eager at startup (unless `@Lazy`) | Lazy — only on demand |
| **Caching** | Cached in singleton registry | Not cached — GC eligible after use |
| **`@PreDestroy` called?** | Yes, on context close | No — client must clean up |
| **Thread safety** | Must be thread-safe | Each caller gets own instance |
| **Memory** | Low (one instance) | Higher (many instances) |
| **Use case** | Services, repos, utils | Commands, forms, builders |

The prototype-into-singleton problem is the most common scope-related bug: when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, the injection happens once at singleton creation time. The singleton holds that single prototype instance forever — defeating the purpose of prototype scope.

Fix this with `ObjectFactory<T>`, `Provider<T>`, `@Lookup`, or scoped proxies. `ObjectFactory.getObject()` calls `getBean()` each time, creating a fresh prototype instance.

sections.title: Decision Guide
sections.content:
Use this mental checklist:

1. **Is the bean stateless?** → Singleton. Services that process data via method parameters don't need multiple instances.
2. **Does it hold per-request data?** → Prototype or request scope. Shopping carts, form validators with state, command objects.
3. **Is it a third-party class that isn't thread-safe?** → Prototype. Wrap it in a factory or use `ObjectFactory<T>`.
4. **Does it need cleanup?** → Be careful with prototype — Spring won't call `@PreDestroy`. Consider singleton with manual scoping.
5. **Is it injected into a singleton?** → If it must be prototype, use `Provider<T>` or `ObjectFactory<T>` instead of direct injection.

In Spring Boot web apps, also consider **request** and **session** scopes before defaulting to prototype — they provide automatic lifecycle management tied to HTTP lifecycle events.

questions.title: Request Scope - HTTP Request Lifecycle Bean
questions.question: What is request scope?

answer.summary: Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request and destroys it when the request completes. It's ideal for request-specific data like form objects, request metadata, and per-request caching.

sections.title: One Bean Per HTTP Request
sections.content:
**Request scope** creates a new bean instance for each incoming HTTP request and destroys it when the request processing completes. The bean is available throughout the entire request lifecycle — across controllers, services, and filters that participate in handling that specific request.

This scope exists only in **web-aware ApplicationContexts** (Spring MVC, Spring WebFlux). It requires the `RequestContextListener` or `RequestContextFilter` to be registered — Spring Boot configures this automatically.

Request scope is useful when you need to carry data across multiple components within a single request without passing it through every method parameter. For example, storing the authenticated user, request timing data, or a request-specific cache that should be discarded after the response is sent.

sections.title: Request-Scoped Beans in Practice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **One instance per HTTP request** — created when the request starts, destroyed when the response is sent; available to all components handling that request
- **Requires scoped proxy for singleton injection** — `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS` injects a CGLIB proxy that delegates to the current request's bean instance
- **`@PreDestroy` IS called** — unlike prototype scope, request-scoped beans get proper destruction callbacks when the request completes
- **Available only in web-aware contexts** — requires `RequestContextListener` or `RequestContextFilter`; Spring Boot auto-configures this
- **Ideal for request-specific data** — trace IDs, authenticated user info, request timing, and per-request caches that should be discarded after the response

sections.content:

To inject a request-scoped bean into a singleton, you need `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`. This creates a CGLIB proxy that delegates each method call to the instance belonging to the current HTTP request. Without the proxy, startup fails because there's no active request when the singleton is created.

Unlike prototype scope, request-scoped beans **do** get `@PreDestroy` callbacks when the request completes. Use request scope for per-request data like trace IDs, authenticated user info, and request-scoped caches. Spring Boot auto-configures the `RequestContextFilter` needed for this scope to work.
