questions.title: Session Scope - HTTP Session Lifecycle Bean
questions.question: What is session scope?

answer.summary: Session scope creates one bean instance per HTTP session, living across multiple requests from the same user. It's suited for user-specific state like shopping carts, preferences, and wizard form data.

sections.title: One Bean Per User Session
sections.content:
**Session scope** creates a bean instance that's tied to an HTTP session and lives for the duration of that session — across multiple requests from the same user. The bean is created on first access within the session and destroyed when the session expires or is invalidated.

Like request scope, session scope is only available in web-aware contexts and requires `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS` when injected into singleton beans. Spring Boot configures the necessary infrastructure automatically.

Session scope is appropriate for data that must persist across multiple requests for the same user but shouldn't be shared between users: shopping carts, multi-step form wizards, user preference caches, and authentication state.

sections.title: Session-Scoped Bean Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- **One instance per HTTP session** — persists across multiple requests from the same user; destroyed when the session expires or is invalidated
- **Implement `Serializable` for clustered environments** — session replication and persistence require serializable session-scoped beans
- **`@PreDestroy` called on session expiry** — fires when the session times out or `session.invalidate()` is called, unlike prototype beans
- **Memory scales with active sessions** — each concurrent user gets their own instance; keep session-scoped beans lightweight to avoid memory pressure
- **Rarely used in REST/stateless APIs** — session scope implies server-side state; prefer JWT tokens or request scope for stateless architectures

questions.title: @Scope Annotation - Defining Bean Scope
questions.question: How do you define bean scope using annotations?

answer.summary: @Scope annotation defines the scope of a Spring bean — singleton, prototype, request, session, or application. It's used on @Component classes or @Bean methods, and can specify a scoped proxy mode for cross-scope injection.

sections.title: Configuring Bean Scope with @Scope
sections.content:
The `@Scope` annotation is how you override Spring's default singleton scope. It can be applied to `@Component` classes (and its stereotypes like `@Service`, `@Repository`) or to `@Bean` methods in `@Configuration` classes.

The annotation accepts two main attributes:
- `value` (or `scopeName`) — the scope name: `"singleton"`, `"prototype"`, `"request"`, `"session"`, `"application"`, or a custom scope name
- `proxyMode` — controls how the bean is exposed when injected into a different-scoped bean. Options are `DEFAULT` (no proxy), `TARGET_CLASS` (CGLIB proxy), and `INTERFACES` (JDK proxy)

Spring provides constants for web scopes in `WebApplicationContext`: `SCOPE_REQUEST`, `SCOPE_SESSION`, `SCOPE_APPLICATION`. Using these constants instead of raw strings prevents typos.

sections.title: @Scope Usage Patterns
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Scope("prototype")` overrides the default singleton** — applied on `@Component` classes or `@Bean` methods to change the bean's lifecycle and instance count
- **`proxyMode` enables cross-scope injection** — `ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS` creates a CGLIB proxy for injecting shorter-lived beans into singletons
- **Use framework constants for safety** — `ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE` and `WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST` prevent typos in string literals
- **`@RequestScope` and `@SessionScope` are shortcuts** — Spring 4.3 meta-annotations that combine scope name with `proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS` in a single annotation
- **Custom scopes are possible** — implement `Scope` interface and register via `ConfigurableBeanFactory.registerScope()` for custom lifecycle management

sections.content:
`@Scope` is the annotation you use to override Spring's default singleton scope. Put it on a `@Component` class or a `@Bean` method with the scope name: `@Scope("prototype")`, `@Scope("request")`, etc. Use framework constants like `ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE` to avoid typos.

The `proxyMode` attribute is critical for cross-scope injection. When injecting a shorter-lived bean into a singleton, set `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS` to create a CGLIB proxy that delegates to the right scoped instance at runtime.

Since Spring 4.3, there are convenient shortcuts: `@RequestScope` and `@SessionScope` combine the scope name with `proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS` in a single annotation. These are the recommended way to declare web scopes — less verbose and less error-prone than the full `@Scope` annotation.

questions.title: Scoped Proxy - Injecting Shorter-Lived Beans
questions.question: What is scoped proxy in Spring?

answer.summary: A scoped proxy wraps a shorter-lived bean (request/session/prototype) so it can be injected into a longer-lived bean (singleton). The proxy delegates each method call to the correct scoped instance at runtime.

sections.title: Why Scoped Proxies Are Necessary
sections.content:
Consider this scenario: a singleton `OrderService` needs a request-scoped `RequestContext`. The singleton is created at startup when there's no HTTP request — so Spring can't inject a request-scoped bean. Even if it could, injecting once would give every request the same instance, defeating the purpose.

**Scoped proxies** solve this by injecting a **proxy object** instead of the actual bean. The proxy looks like the target bean (implements the same interface or extends the same class), but each method call on the proxy is transparently delegated to the correct scoped instance for the current context (current request, current session, etc.).

The proxy uses thread-local context to find the right instance. For request scope, it looks up the bean in the current HTTP request's attributes. For session scope, it looks in the current HTTP session. This happens on every method call, ensuring the correct instance is always used.

questions.title: Dependency Injection - DI Pattern in Spring
questions.question: What is Dependency Injection?

answer.summary: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external source (the Spring container) rather than creating them internally, enabling loose coupling and testability.

sections.title: What Is Dependency Injection
sections.content:
**Dependency Injection (DI)** is a design pattern that implements **Inversion of Control (IoC)** — instead of a class creating its own dependencies, they are "injected" by an external entity (the Spring IoC container). This inverts the traditional control flow where classes are responsible for obtaining their own collaborators.

Without DI, classes are tightly coupled to their dependencies:
```java
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway = new StripeGateway(); // tightly coupled
}
```

With DI, the dependency is provided from outside:
```java
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway; // interface, not implementation
    public OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }
}
```

This simple change delivers three major benefits:
1. **Loose coupling** — `OrderService` depends on the `PaymentGateway` interface, not `StripeGateway`. You can swap implementations without changing `OrderService`.
2. **Testability** — in unit tests, inject a mock `PaymentGateway` instead of hitting real payment APIs.
3. **Configuration flexibility** — the Spring container decides which implementation to inject based on configuration, profiles, or conditions.

sections.title: How Spring Implements DI
sections.content:
Spring's IoC container manages the entire DI lifecycle:

1. **Bean Definition** — Spring reads `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Bean`, or XML configurations to learn what beans exist and what they need.
2. **Dependency Resolution** — For each bean, Spring identifies its dependencies (constructor parameters, `@Autowired` fields) and resolves them by type or name.
3. **Instantiation** — Spring creates beans in the correct order — dependencies are created before the beans that need them.
4. **Injection** — Dependencies are passed to the bean via constructor, setter, or field injection.

Spring resolves dependencies **by type** first. If multiple beans of the same type exist, it falls back to **by name** (matching the parameter/field name to a bean name). If that's still ambiguous, you use `@Qualifier` or `@Primary` to disambiguate.

The container handles circular dependencies in some cases (setter injection), but fails fast for constructor-based circular dependencies — which is generally the right behavior since circular dependencies often indicate a design problem.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IoC inverts who creates dependencies** — instead of `new PaymentGateway()` inside the service, the Spring container creates and provides it from outside
- **Program to interfaces, not implementations** — DI naturally encourages depending on abstractions; swap implementations without changing consumer code
- **Enables unit testing with mocks** — inject `MockPaymentGateway` in tests instead of hitting real APIs; no Spring context needed for constructor injection
- **Spring resolves by type, then by name** — `@Autowired` first matches by type; if ambiguous, falls back to parameter/field name matching, then `@Qualifier`
- **Three injection types: constructor, setter, field** — constructor is recommended for required deps (immutable, testable), setter for optional, field is discouraged

questions.title: Types of Dependency Injection - Constructor, Setter, Field
questions.question: What are the types of Dependency Injection in Spring?

answer.summary: Spring supports three DI types: constructor injection (recommended — immutable, testable), setter injection (optional dependencies), and field injection (concise but untestable, discouraged).

sections.title: Three Ways to Inject Dependencies
sections.content:
Spring provides three mechanisms for dependency injection, each with distinct trade-offs. The Spring team officially recommends **constructor injection** for required dependencies and **setter injection** for optional ones. Field injection, while widely used, is discouraged in modern Spring development.

The choice affects your code's testability, immutability, and clarity about what a class requires. Let's examine each approach in detail.

sections.title: DI Types Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | Constructor | Setter | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@Autowired` needed? | No (single constructor) | Yes | Yes |
| **Immutability** | Yes (`final` fields) | No | No |
| **Required deps** | Enforced (compile-time) | Optional by default | No enforcement |
| **Testability** | Easy (pass via constructor) | Moderate (call setters) | Hard (needs reflection) |
| **Circular deps** | Fails fast (good) | Allowed (risky) | Allowed (risky) |
| **Readability** | Clear contract | Scattered setters | Hidden dependencies |

sections.title: Each Injection Type in Code
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Constructor injection creates immutable objects** — `final` fields guarantee thread safety and make dependencies explicit in the constructor signature
- **Setter injection handles optional dependencies** — `@Autowired(required = false)` on setters allows the bean to function without the dependency
- **Field injection is discouraged** — requires reflection, can't use `final`, impossible to unit test without Spring or reflection frameworks
- **Single constructor doesn't need `@Autowired`** — since Spring 4.3, a class with one constructor is automatically used for injection without any annotation
- **Too many constructor params signals design issues** — more than 5-6 dependencies usually means the class has too many responsibilities and should be split

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring supports three injection types. **Constructor injection** is the recommended approach — dependencies are passed via the constructor, can be `final` for immutability, and the class can never exist in an invalid state. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor doesn't even need `@Autowired`.

**Setter injection** is for optional dependencies — annotate a setter with `@Autowired(required = false)` and the bean works even if the dependency isn't available. It allows reconfiguration after construction.

**Field injection** (`@Autowired` on a field) is the most concise but the most problematic — fields can't be `final`, and you can't test the class without Spring or reflection because there's no constructor or setter to pass dependencies through. The Spring team explicitly discourages field injection. A good rule: if your constructor gets too long (5+ parameters), that's not a reason to switch to field injection — it's a signal to split the class.

questions.title: Constructor Injection vs Setter Injection - Best Practices
questions.question: What is the difference between constructor and setter injection?

answer.summary: Constructor injection enforces required dependencies with immutable fields (recommended by Spring). Setter injection handles optional dependencies that have defaults. Never mix required dependencies into setter injection.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Injection Style
sections.content:
The Spring team's official recommendation is clear: **use constructor injection for mandatory dependencies** and **setter injection for optional dependencies** that have sensible defaults. This isn't just a style preference — it affects correctness, safety, and testability.

Constructor injection creates **immutable objects** with `final` fields. Once constructed, the bean's dependencies cannot change — this makes it inherently thread-safe and eliminates an entire category of bugs where dependencies are accidentally overwritten or left null. It also makes the dependency contract explicit: the constructor signature tells you exactly what a class needs to function.

Setter injection allows dependencies to be **reconfigured after construction** — the bean starts with default values and setters allow overriding them. This is appropriate for optional collaborators, configurable strategies, or legacy code that needs to support null dependencies gracefully.

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content:
| Scenario | Use Constructor | Use Setter |
|---|---|---|
| Required dependency | Yes — won't compile without it | No — bean can be in invalid state |
| Optional dependency with default | No — constructor must always accept it | Yes — only call setter when overriding |
| Immutable bean | Yes — `final` fields | No — fields must be mutable |
| Circular dependency | Fails (redesign needed) | Works (Spring injects proxy) |
| Third-party class you can't modify | No | Yes — configure via `@Bean` method |
| Unit testing without Spring | Easy — `new Service(mockA, mockB)` | Moderate — create, then call setters |

questions.title: @Autowired Annotation - Automatic Dependency Injection
questions.question: What is @Autowired annotation?

answer.summary: @Autowired tells Spring to automatically inject a matching bean by type. Since Spring 4.3, it's optional on single constructors. It works on constructors, setters, fields, and even arbitrary methods.

sections.title: Automatic Dependency Resolution
sections.content:
`@Autowired` is Spring's annotation for automatic dependency injection. When Spring sees `@Autowired`, it searches the container for a bean matching the required type and injects it. If no matching bean exists, startup fails with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` (unless `required = false`).

Since Spring 4.3, `@Autowired` is **optional on single constructors** — if a class has exactly one constructor, Spring automatically uses it for injection. This is why modern Spring code often has no `@Autowired` annotations at all when using constructor injection.

`@Autowired` resolution follows this order:
1. **Match by type** — find beans of the required type
2. **Narrow by qualifier** — if `@Qualifier` is present, filter by name
3. **Match by field/parameter name** — if multiple candidates, try matching the field name to a bean name
4. **Use `@Primary`** — if one candidate is marked `@Primary`, select it
5. **Fail** — if still ambiguous, throw `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`

sections.content:
- **Resolves by type first, then by name** — finds beans of the matching type; if multiple exist, tries matching field/parameter name to bean name before failing

- **Works on constructors, setters, fields, and methods** — most flexible on constructors (recommended) and setters (optional deps); field injection is concise but untestable
- **`List<T>` and `Map<String, T>` inject all matching beans** — `List<NotificationChannel>` collects all implementations; `Map` gives bean names as keys
- **`@Primary` and `@Qualifier` resolve ambiguity** — `@Primary` marks the default bean; `@Qualifier("name")` explicitly selects a specific bean at the injection point

sections.content:
By default, `@Autowired` is `required = true` — if Spring can't find a matching bean, the application fails to start. Setting `required = false` tells Spring that the dependency is optional: if a matching bean exists, inject it; if not, leave the field as `null` (or don't call the setter method).

This is useful when a feature is conditionally available. For example, a caching layer might be optional — if a `CacheManager` bean is configured, use it; otherwise, fall through to direct database access. Or a metrics system might be present in production but absent in tests.

Since Spring 5, you have three ways to express optional dependencies:
1. `@Autowired(required = false)` — field is `null` if no bean found
2. `Optional<T>` — wraps the bean in `Optional.empty()` if absent (cleaner, no null checks)
3. `@Nullable` (from JSR-305 or Spring's own) — same as `required = false` but annotation-based

sections.title: Three Ways to Handle Optional Dependencies
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`required=false` prevents startup failure** — if no matching bean exists, the field stays `null` instead of throwing `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`
- **`Optional<T>` is the modern alternative** — wraps the dependency in `Optional.empty()` when absent; cleaner than null checks with `ifPresent()` and `orElse()`
- **`@Nullable` achieves the same effect** — Spring's `@Nullable` or JSR-305 `@Nullable` on a parameter makes the injection optional without `required=false`
- **Always null-check before use** — `required=false` fields can be `null`; calling methods on them without checking causes `NullPointerException` at runtime
- **Use for conditional features** — caching, metrics, audit logging, and other features that may not be configured in all environments

questions.title: @Qualifier Annotation - Resolving Ambiguity
questions.question: What is @Qualifier annotation?

answer.summary: @Qualifier narrows bean selection when multiple candidates of the same type exist. It works with @Autowired to select by bean name or custom qualifier, resolving NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

sections.title: Resolving Ambiguity with @Qualifier
sections.content:
When Spring's `@Autowired` finds multiple beans of the same type, it throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. The `@Qualifier` annotation resolves this ambiguity by specifying **which** bean to inject by its name or a custom qualifier value.

This situation is common in practice: you might have multiple `DataSource` beans (primary DB and read replica), multiple `RestTemplate` instances (one per external API), or multiple implementations of a strategy interface.

Spring provides three mechanisms to resolve ambiguity, in order of preference:
1. `@Primary` — marks one bean as the default choice (applied to the bean definition)
2. `@Qualifier("name")` — selects a specific bean by name (applied at the injection point)
3. **Parameter/field name matching** — Spring tries to match the field name to a bean name as a last resort

`@Qualifier` takes precedence over `@Primary` — if both are present, `@Qualifier` wins. Use `@Primary` when one bean should be the default for most injection points, and `@Qualifier` for specific injection points that need a different bean.

sections.title: @Qualifier and @Primary in Practice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Selects by bean name when type is ambiguous** — `@Qualifier("replicaDs")` picks the specific `DataSource` bean named "replicaDs" from multiple candidates
- **Takes precedence over `@Primary`** — if both `@Primary` and `@Qualifier` apply, `@Qualifier` wins at that injection point while `@Primary` remains the default elsewhere
- **Custom qualifier annotations are type-safe** — define `@ReadOnly` meta-annotated with `@Qualifier` for compile-time safety and refactoring support
- **Works on constructors, fields, and setters** — place `@Qualifier` on the parameter or field alongside `@Autowired` to narrow the candidate set
- **`@Primary` is the simpler alternative** — when one bean should be the default for most injection points, `@Primary` avoids scattering `@Qualifier` everywhere

sections.content:

`@Qualifier` takes precedence over `@Primary`. Use `@Primary` when one bean should be the default for most injection points, and `@Qualifier` for specific injection points that need a different bean. For example, mark the primary database as `@Primary` and use `@Qualifier("replicaDs")` only in the reporting service that reads from the replica.

For type safety, you can create **custom qualifier annotations** — define an annotation like `@ReadOnly` that's meta-annotated with `@Qualifier`. This gives you compile-time safety and refactoring support instead of relying on strings that can have typos.

questions.title: Circular Dependency - Dependency Loop Problem
questions.question: What is circular dependency in Spring?

answer.summary: Circular dependency occurs when bean A depends on bean B which depends on bean A, creating a cycle. With constructor injection, Spring fails fast; with field/setter injection, Spring may resolve it using early references.

sections.title: Understanding Circular Dependencies
sections.content:
A **circular dependency** (or dependency loop) occurs when two or more beans depend on each other, directly or indirectly, creating a cycle that Spring cannot resolve. The simplest case: `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` in its constructor, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` in its constructor. Spring can't create either one first because each requires the other to already exist.

Circular dependencies are almost always a **design problem** — they indicate that responsibilities are poorly separated or that two classes are too tightly coupled. Before reaching for a technical fix, consider refactoring: extract the shared logic into a third class, use events for decoupling, or rethink the class boundaries.

Spring's behavior depends on the injection type:
- **Constructor injection** → `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup. This is the **desirable** outcome — it forces you to fix the design.
- **Setter/field injection** → Spring may resolve it by injecting an early reference (a partially initialized bean). This "works" but is fragile — the injected bean hasn't finished initialization, which can cause `NullPointerException` at runtime.

sections.title: How Spring Detects and (Sometimes) Resolves Cycles
sections.content:
When Spring creates a singleton bean, it adds it to a "currently in creation" set. If, during dependency resolution, it encounters a bean that's already in this set, it has detected a cycle.

For constructor injection cycles, Spring fails immediately — there's no safe way to provide a partially constructed object because the constructor hasn't returned yet.

For setter/field injection, Spring uses a **three-level cache** (singleton cache, early singleton factory, singleton factory) to break the cycle. It creates Bean A's instance (just the constructor), registers an early reference, then creates Bean B (injecting A's early reference), then finishes A's initialization. This works but means B receives a reference to A before A's `@PostConstruct` has run.

Since Spring Boot 2.6, circular dependencies cause startup failure by default even with setter injection. You must explicitly opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`, which is Spring's way of discouraging this pattern.

Signs of circular dependency problems:
- `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup
- `NullPointerException` in `@PostConstruct` methods (partially initialized bean)
- Unpredictable initialization order

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Bean A needs B, B needs A** — creates an unsolvable chicken-and-egg problem when both use constructor injection; Spring throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`
- **Constructor injection fails fast (good)** — the error at startup forces you to fix the design rather than hiding it behind partial initialization
- **Setter/field injection may silently resolve** — Spring injects early references to partially-initialized beans, risking `NullPointerException` in `@PostConstruct` methods
- **Spring Boot 2.6+ disallows all circular deps by default** — `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` re-enables the old behavior, but fixing the design is better
- **Usually signals a design problem** — circular dependencies indicate two classes are too tightly coupled; extract shared logic into a third class to break the cycle

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **circular dependency** happens when bean A depends on bean B and bean B depends on bean A — neither can be created first. With constructor injection, Spring detects this immediately and throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup, which is actually the best outcome because it forces you to fix the design.

With setter or field injection, Spring can sometimes resolve the cycle by injecting an **early reference** — a partially initialized bean. Bean A is created (constructor only), its reference is saved, Bean B is created with A's reference, then A's setters are called with B. This works but is fragile — B receives A before A's `@PostConstruct` has run.

Since **Spring Boot 2.6**, circular dependencies are disallowed by default even with setter injection. You can re-enable them with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`, but the better approach is to redesign: usually circular dependencies mean two classes are too tightly coupled and the shared logic should be extracted into a third class.

questions.title: Resolve Circular Dependency - @Lazy and Setter Injection
questions.question: How do you resolve circular dependency in Spring?

answer.summary: Resolve circular dependencies by redesigning (extracting shared logic), using @Lazy to inject a proxy, switching to setter injection, or using events/interfaces to decouple. Redesigning is always the best solution.

sections.title: Strategies for Breaking Dependency Cycles
sections.content:
When you encounter a circular dependency, the first question should be: **is the design correct?** Most circular dependencies indicate a class is doing too much or two classes are too tightly coupled. The best fix is usually architectural, not technical.

That said, here are the solutions in order of preference:

1. **Redesign** — Extract shared logic into a third class that both depend on (unidirectional). This eliminates the cycle entirely and usually produces better code.
2. **Use events** — Replace direct method calls with `ApplicationEventPublisher`. A publishes an event, B listens — no direct dependency.
3. **Use `@Lazy`** — Annotate one injection point with `@Lazy`. Spring injects a proxy that creates the real bean on first use, breaking the construction-time cycle.
4. **Use setter injection** — Move one dependency from constructor to setter (not recommended since Spring Boot 2.6 disallows by default).
5. **Use `ObjectFactory<T>` or `Provider<T>`** — Defer bean lookup to runtime instead of construction time.

sections.title: Solutions in Code
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Redesign is the best solution** — extract shared logic into a new class that both depend on unidirectionally, eliminating the cycle entirely
- **`@Lazy` injects a proxy to break the cycle** — the proxy defers real bean creation to first method call, allowing both beans to finish construction
- **Events decouple direct references** — replace `orderService.notify()` with `publisher.publishEvent(new OrderEvent())` to remove the bidirectional dependency
- **`ObjectFactory<T>` defers lookup to runtime** — `objectFactory.getObject()` resolves the bean when called, not at construction time
- **Setter injection is the weakest fix** — it allows circular deps by injecting early references, but the bean may not be fully initialized, causing subtle bugs

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The best solution is always to **redesign**: if `OrderService` and `PaymentService` depend on each other, extract the shared logic into an `OrderPaymentCoordinator` that both depend on unidirectionally. This eliminates the cycle and usually produces better code.

If redesigning isn't practical, use **`@Lazy`** on one injection point — Spring injects a proxy that defers real bean creation to the first method call, breaking the construction-time cycle. Another option is **events**: replace `paymentService.process()` with `publisher.publishEvent(new OrderEvent())` and have `PaymentService` listen via `@EventListener`.

Technically, you can also use **`ObjectFactory<T>`** to defer bean lookup to runtime, or switch one side to **setter injection**. But setter injection is the weakest fix — Spring Boot 2.6+ disallows it by default, and it can cause subtle bugs with partially initialized beans. When you find yourself needing circular dependency workarounds, treat it as a design smell.
